text: Welcome to the capstone. Everything you've learned across the last eight chapters — control flow, data flow, variables, error handling, incremental loads, deployment — is about to get used in one real package, built across the next four lessons. This one isn't a toy example. It extracts from a real transactional database and loads into a real dimensional target, the same two databases this catalog's other courses already use.

The shape of this project is Extract, Transform, Load, and Log — four stages, and this chapter adds one more on top of each lesson before it. Extract pulls order data out of a real OLTP source. Transform reshapes those rows, resolving the source system's business keys into warehouse surrogate keys along the way. Load lands the result in a small dimensional target built specifically for this capstone. And Log — which Lesson 48 adds — records what happened on every single run, so the package is something you'd actually trust to run unattended. Lesson 47 gets Extract, Transform, and Load working end to end; Lesson 48 adds Log, plus makes the whole thing incremental and resilient to bad rows; Lesson 49 wraps it into something you can show off.

The source is AdventureWorks2012 — three ordinary transactional tables: SalesOrderHeader, SalesOrderDetail, and Product. No dimensional shape, no surrogate keys, just the rows a real sales system writes every day. The target is new: two small tables you'll create yourself inside AdventureWorksDW2014, called CapstoneDimProduct and CapstoneFactOrderSales. They're deliberately separate from that database's real DimProduct and FactInternetSales tables, so this project can't collide with anything else. The one thing you don't build yourself is the date dimension — AdventureWorksDW2014 already has a correct DimDate table, and the capstone's fact table joins straight to it.

Before Lesson 47, get both sides ready: create the two Capstone tables in AdventureWorksDW2014, and set up a new Integration Services project with connection managers pointed at both databases. Next lesson, we build the actual control flow and data flow — for real, end to end.
